fixes.explanation: The text says they can't. "…the Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them." (Judges 20:34) The battle is fierce, and they still don't see it. Only later does the text say they realized they had been defeated (Judges 20:36).

Judah went first at the start (Judges 20:18), but the text names someone else here. "The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel…" (Judges 20:35) He's the one it credits. That matches what the LORD had answered them before: "Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand." (Judges 20:28)

They are. The men of Israel turn back on them, and "…the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them." (Judges 41) Terrified is the text's own word. Then they flee before the men of Israel toward the wilderness (Judges 20:42).
They say it together: "Not one of us will return to his tent or to his house." (Judges 20:8) That's a big promise from the crowd gathered at Mizpah. Nobody is slipping out the back.

Chariots, huh? Somebody's been watching too many movies, friend. The men from every tribe are chosen to supply provisions for the army when it goes to Gibeah (Judges 20:10). This is a supply run, not a parade.

Arrows and a ring? Nice try, friend, but that's a different skill. The text says each of the 700 select left-handers could sling a stone at a hair without missing (Judges 20:16). Slingers, not archers, and their target was a hair, which makes a ring look like easy mode.

A spear across a river? Friend, these men weren't aiming at anything that big. The text says each of the 700 select left-handers could sling a stone at a hair without missing (Judges 20:16). A hair is a much smaller target than a river.
The text doesn't describe them that way. It says these swordsmen were each one an experienced warrior (Judges 20:17). Farmers aren't what it names.

The text has Benjamin coming out and starting the attack. The Benjamites come out against them, are drawn away from the city and begin to attack the people as before (Judges 20:31). Israel had set up an ambush around Gibeah (Judges 20:29), but this verse shows Benjamin as the one attacking.

The text has no waiting in it. The Benjamites come out and begin to attack as before, killing about thirty men of Israel in the fields and on the roads (Judges 20:31). That's fighting, not standing around.

The text doesn't show the ambush marching away. The men in ambush had rushed against Gibeah (Judges 20:37), and when the column of smoke goes up, the Benjamites look behind them and see the whole city going up in smoke (Judges 20:40). That's what's in their view.
The text doesn't mention any help coming. The Benjamites look behind them and see the whole city going up in smoke (Judges 20:40). Smoke is what they see, not friends.

That's what the text says. The men of Israel turned back on them, and "…the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them." (Judges 20:41) Earlier the Benjamites had said, "They are defeated before us as in the first battle." (Judges 20:39)
That's where the 600 go. The text says they "…turned and fled into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon…" (Judges 20:47) That's the place the text names.
They stayed there four months (Judges 20:47). That's a long stretch to stay in one spot. The text only says they stayed, and I won't guess what those months were like.
